abstract_zh: 本更新综述总结了近年来对人类免疫应答、发病机制和疫苗发展的理解进展,特别关注中国独特的流行病学情况。本综述识别了研究空白并提出了未来方向,强调需要多价疫苗、改进的诊断方法以及整合的监测系统。本综述聚焦于中国四种临床重要的虫媒病毒(DENV、ZIKV、JEV和CHIKV),探讨了近期对保护性免疫、发病机制和疫苗发展的理解进展,同时应对中国特有的流行病学挑战,包括多种登革热血清型的共循环、基孔肯雅热输入病例的增加,以及在气候变暖背景下对整合媒介 监测系统的需求[13,14,15,16]。摘要 虫媒病毒一直是公共卫生的持续挑战,其影响因气候变化、全球化和媒介扩展而加剧。截至2026年,中国面临由蚊媒病毒带来的不断演变的威胁,包括登革热(DENV)、寨卡病毒(ZIKV)、日本脑炎(JEV)和基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)。我们分析了临床结果,识别了关键的保护性免疫相关因素和疾病增强因素,并系统评估了2010年至2026年间疫苗候选疫苗。值得注意的是,美国食品药品监督管理局(FDA)批准的CHIKV疫苗Ixchiq是一个里程碑,但登革热和寨卡病毒的免疫策略仍面临挑战。我们讨论了中国在气候驱动的媒介扩展、跨境传播风险以及成功实施的JEV 疫苗接种项目中获得的关键经验教训。1 引言 虫媒病毒的出现和再出现继续对全球公共卫生构成重大威胁[1]。截至2026年中旬,中国面临由蚊媒病毒带来的不断演变的威胁,包括登革热(DENV)、寨卡病毒(ZIKV)、日本脑炎(JEV)和基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述聚焦于中国四种临床重要的虫媒病毒(DENV、ZIKV、JEV和CHIKV),探讨了近期对保护性免疫、发病机制和疫苗发展的理解进展,同时应对中国特有的流行病学挑战,包括多种登革热血清型的共循环、基孔肯雅热输入病例的增加,以及在气候变暖背景下对整合媒介 监测系统的需求[13,14,15,16]。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 综述包括2024年至2026年间发表的研究证据,特别关注中国特定的数据。它讨论了基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)的流行病学状况、血清型分布和临床表现,以及气候变化对媒介栖息地和疾病传播的影响。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 由于先前暴露模式的不同,基础免疫力的异质性对ADE风险和疫苗部署策略具有影响。此外,综述还强调了需要改进诊断方法和整合监测系统,以应对基孔肯雅病毒和其他虫媒病毒在中国不断演变的威胁。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 综述强调需要多价疫苗、改进的诊断方法和整合的监测系统,以应对基孔肯雅病毒和其他虫媒病毒在中国带来的挑战。它还呼吁进一步研究血清型/谱系结构、复制动力学以及宿主免疫相互作用,这些因素塑造了疾病结果和公共卫生策略。

title: Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications

source_records.title: Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications
Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications

priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
full_text: ABSTRACTThe Amapa State, Brazil, in the Amazon region and bordering French Guiana, is a strategic sentinel location for infectious disease surveillance. Ecological pressures such as deforestation, artisanal gold mining, and high human mobility contribute to complex transmission dynamics of arboviruses, bacterial infections, and other pathogens. This study aims to characterize the etiologies of acute febrile illness (AFI) reported in Amapa State in 2018-2020, focusing on arbovirus circulation, bacterial contributions, and emerging pathogens. A retrospective analysis was carried out with 727 AFI cases. Laboratory diagnoses were established using molecular and serological assays, with systematic testing for different pathogens. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection. Dengue virus was the predominant etiological agent (n=109, 52%), followed by leptospirosis (n=20, 9.5%), chikungunya virus (n=16, 7.6%), parvovirus B19 (n=16, 7.6%), measles (n=15, 7.1%), zika virus (n=10, 4.8%), mayaro virus (n=1,0.5%), and other bacterial infections (n=5, 2.4%). Isolated cases of hepatitis A and B, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, enterovirus, and acute Chagas disease were also identified. No hepatitis E virus or oropouche cases were detected. Dengue virus was the leading cause of AFI. Leptospirosis, chikungunya virus, and parvovirus B19 were other prevalent and often underrecognized contributors. The detection of additional viruses highlights Amapa State as a potential zone of “silent expansion” for emerging arboviruses. Co-detection of multiple pathogens underscores diagnostic complexity in regions with overlapping transmission. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide public health interventions.KEYWORDS: Dengue, Leptospirosis, Arbovirus infections, Chikungunya fever, Parvovirus B19 MATERIAL AND METHODSStudy design and populationAn observational, cross-sectional, retrospective, and descriptive study was conducted using a convenience sample. Serum specimens were collected from patients presenting with AFI during routine diagnostic procedures in public health laboratories. Samples from 727 individuals, collected in 2018 (n = 20), 2019 (n = 581), and 2020 (n = 126), were analyzed.This study aims to find the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in AFI cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil. AFI, with a fever duration cutoff of 2-7 day from onset, was chosen as the inclusion criterion.Laboratory proceduresSpecimens were initially processed at the Central Public Health Laboratory of Amapa State (LACEN-AP) following routine diagnostic protocols, including arbovirus screening when clinically indicated. Additional tests, such as serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for other pathogens, were performed at the discretion of attending physicians, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory local methods included enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (the latter exclusively for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing; for bacterial and fungal infections, ELISA for leptospirosis and blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed; whereas parasitic infections were confirmed using thick blood smears, the Strout test, electrochemiluminescence, and immunochromatographic tests.After initial processing, samples were stored at −20 °C and shipped to the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP, LIM-52), in which they were preserved at −80 °C until further testing.Molecular screeningAt LV-IMT-FMUSP, samples underwent real-time PCR assays targeting viral agents. The screening included assays for Pan-Orthoflavivirus and Pan-Alphavirus. The following viral agents were tested: Flaviviruses, Alphaviruses, Orthobunyaviruses: yellow fever 8 , dengue, zika, chikungunya, mayaro, and oropouche viruses 9 .Genus Orthoflavivirus 10 : Japanese encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Usutu, West Nile, and Saint Louis encephalitis viruses.Genus Alphavirus 11 : Ross River, O’nyong-nyong, Sindbis, Barmah Forest, Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses. Additional real-time PCR assays included pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations, such as enterovirus 12 , parvovirus B19 13 , hepatitis E virus (HEV) 14 , and Leptospira spp 15 .GALIn this study, diagnostic test results from LACEN-AP were retrieved via GAL.GAL, the national computerized system, was designed to manage and monitor laboratory routines within the National Public Health Laboratory Network. It is managed by the Ministry of Health via the General Coordination of Public Health Laboratories and tracks the flow of biological samples from collection to final diagnosis, standardizing results and providing real-time data for the surveillance of high-priority and compulsory notification diseases.SINANSINAN, the primary national surveillance database managed by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, is a decentralized system fed by the mandatory notification of diseases and conditions in the National Compulsory Notification List.SINAN provides high-resolution microdata (individual-level records) that include clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, pregnancy status, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations), diagnostic test results, among others.Integration of dataClinical and demographic variables (age, sex, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations) were combined with GAL laboratory results. Using this integrated dataset, data analysis was strictly descriptive, focusing on characterizing the reported cases.For the diagnostic tests either at LACEN or IMT, samples were classified as positive if they were reactive in at least one assay.Statistical analysisContinuous variables are shown as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR), and categorical ones, as frequencies. Subgroup pairwise comparisons were performed via the Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Correlation between monthly cases and NASA POWER precipitation data was assessed using Spearman’s rank test. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate across multiple comparisons. Spatial distribution maps were generated using the geobr, sf, and ggplot2 packages. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, using R(version 4.4.0) via RStudio. Study design and populationAn observational, cross-sectional, retrospective, and descriptive study was conducted using a convenience sample. Serum specimens were collected from patients presenting with AFI during routine diagnostic procedures in public health laboratories. Samples from 727 individuals, collected in 2018 (n = 20), 2019 (n = 581), and 2020 (n = 126), were analyzed.This study aims to find the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in AFI cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTThe Amapa State, Brazil, in the Amazon region and bordering French Guiana, is a strategic sentinel location for infectious disease surveillance. Ecological pressures such as deforestation, artisanal gold mining, and high human mobility contribute to complex transmission dynamics of arboviruses, bacterial infections, and other pathogens. This study aims to characterize the etiologies of acute febrile illness (AFI) reported in Amapa State in 2018-2020, focusing on arbovirus circulation, bacterial contributions, and emerging pathogens. A retrospective analysis was carried out with 727 AFI cases. Laboratory diagnoses were established using molecular and serological assays, with systematic testing for different pathogens. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection. Dengue virus was the predominant etiological agent (n=109, 52%), followed by leptospirosis (n=20, 9.5%), chikungunya virus (n=16, 7.6%), parvovirus B19 (n=16, 7.6%), measles (n=15, 7.1%), zika virus (n=10, 4.8%), mayaro virus (n=1,0.5%), and other bacterial infections (n=5, 2.4%). Isolated cases of hepatitis A and B, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, enterovirus, and acute Chagas disease were also identified. No hepatitis E virus or oropouche cases were detected. Dengue virus was the leading cause of AFI. Leptospirosis, chikungunya virus, and parvovirus B19 were other prevalent and often underrecognized contributors. The detection of additional viruses highlights Amapa State as a potential zone of “silent expansion” for emerging arboviruses. Co-detection of multiple pathogens underscores diagnostic complexity in regions with overlapping transmission. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide public health interventions.KEYWORDS: Dengue, Leptospirosis, Arbovirus infections, Chikungunya fever, Parvovirus B19
full_text_sections.methods: MATERIAL AND METHODSStudy design and populationAn observational, cross-sectional, retrospective, and descriptive study was conducted using a convenience sample. Serum specimens were collected from patients presenting with AFI during routine diagnostic procedures in public health laboratories. Samples from 727 individuals, collected in 2018 (n = 20), 2019 (n = 581), and 2020 (n = 126), were analyzed.This study aims to find the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in AFI cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil. AFI, with a fever duration cutoff of 2-7 day from onset, was chosen as the inclusion criterion.Laboratory proceduresSpecimens were initially processed at the Central Public Health Laboratory of Amapa State (LACEN-AP) following routine diagnostic protocols, including arbovirus screening when clinically indicated. Additional tests, such as serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for other pathogens, were performed at the discretion of attending physicians, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory local methods included enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (the latter exclusively for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing; for bacterial and fungal infections, ELISA for leptospirosis and blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed; whereas parasitic infections were confirmed using thick blood smears, the Strout test, electrochemiluminescence, and immunochromatographic tests.After initial processing, samples were stored at −20 °C and shipped to the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP, LIM-52), in which they were preserved at −80 °C until further testing.Molecular screeningAt LV-IMT-FMUSP, samples underwent real-time PCR assays targeting viral agents. The screening included assays for Pan-Orthoflavivirus and Pan-Alphavirus. The following viral agents were tested: Flaviviruses, Alphaviruses, Orthobunyaviruses: yellow fever 8 , dengue, zika, chikungunya, mayaro, and oropouche viruses 9 .Genus Orthoflavivirus 10 : Japanese encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Usutu, West Nile, and Saint Louis encephalitis viruses.Genus Alphavirus 11 : Ross River, O’nyong-nyong, Sindbis, Barmah Forest, Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses. Additional real-time PCR assays included pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations, such as enterovirus 12 , parvovirus B19 13 , hepatitis E virus (HEV) 14 , and Leptospira spp 15 .GALIn this study, diagnostic test results from LACEN-AP were retrieved via GAL.GAL, the national computerized system, was designed to manage and monitor laboratory routines within the National Public Health Laboratory Network. It is managed by the Ministry of Health via the General Coordination of Public Health Laboratories and tracks the flow of biological samples from collection to final diagnosis, standardizing results and providing real-time data for the surveillance of high-priority and compulsory notification diseases.SINANSINAN, the primary national surveillance database managed by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, is a decentralized system fed by the mandatory notification of diseases and conditions in the National Compulsory Notification List.SINAN provides high-resolution microdata (individual-level records) that include clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, pregnancy status, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations), diagnostic test results, among others.Integration of dataClinical and demographic variables (age, sex, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations) were combined with GAL laboratory results. Using this integrated dataset, data analysis was strictly descriptive, focusing on characterizing the reported cases.For the diagnostic tests either at LACEN or IMT, samples were classified as positive if they were reactive in at least one assay.Statistical analysisContinuous variables are shown as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR), and categorical ones, as frequencies. Subgroup pairwise comparisons were performed via the Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Correlation between monthly cases and NASA POWER precipitation data was assessed using Spearman’s rank test. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate across multiple comparisons. Spatial distribution maps were generated using the geobr, sf, and ggplot2 packages. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, using R(version 4.4.0) via RStudio. Study design and populationAn observational, cross-sectional, retrospective, and descriptive study was conducted using a convenience sample. Serum specimens were collected from patients presenting with AFI during routine diagnostic procedures in public health laboratories. Samples from 727 individuals, collected in 2018 (n = 20), 2019 (n = 581), and 2020 (n = 126), were analyzed.This study aims to find the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in AFI cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil. AFI, with a fever duration cutoff of 2-7 day from onset, was chosen as the inclusion criterion.

full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThis study investigated the etiologies of AFI cases reported in Amapa State from 2018 to 2022. Of 727 evaluated individuals, definitive diagnoses established 185 cases (25.4%), including 23 cases of co-infection.Our findings are in line with previous regional studies. Dengue remains the predominant AFI etiological agent in Latin America, with chikungunya and zika showing an increased prevalence. Leptospirosis, though often overlooked, represents a prevalent bacterial contributor1,16.Notably, this study found one case of mayaro virus infection, consistent with its rare occurrence in Amapa State (six confirmed cases nationwide in 2015-2025) 17 . Following systematic PCR testing, no individual in our cohort was positive for Oropouche virus disease, despite epidemiological data (2015-2025) reporting 16,571 cases nationwide, including 218 in Amapa State. A recent increase in its detection (2023-2024) likely reflects greater diagnostic capacity and active case-finding 17 . These results suggest Amapa State may represent a zone of “silent expansion” for Oropouche virus disease, in which overlapping arbovirus transmission obscures true disease burden. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide interventions. While multiplex syndromic panels are ideal, widespread molecular testing faces strict budget and logistical constraints within the public health system in Amapa State. A more sustainable solution could be a tiered “reflex testing” cascade at LACEN-AP. Under this protocol, a negative molecular result for primary arboviruses (dengue/zika/chikungunya) would automatically trigger reflex testing for leptospirosis and parvovirus B19 using the original biological sample. This flow could optimize laboratory resources, cut costs, and bypass initial clinical triage blind spots without requiring secondary patient appointments. Lessons from the Amazon highlight the global importance of integrated arbovirus surveillance in regions with overlapping transmission.The fact that 80.5% of initial hypotheses were generically classified as suspected arboviruses exposes a profound “dengue-centric” bias. Because the early symptoms of dengue, parvovirus B19, and leptospirosis overlap almost entirely, physical triage alone is insufficient. To address this, the regional health system must implement targeted continuing medical education focusing on broad syndromic classifications—such as “acute exanthematous febrile syndrome”—rather than single-pathogen guessing. Furthermore, standard patient intake forms should mandate structured epidemiological risk questions regarding recent floodwater exposure (leptospirosis), mining or forest exposure (malaria/arboviruses), and artisanal acai consumption (acute Chagas disease) to guide clinical suspicion before laboratory results are available.Leptospirosis remains a critical public health challenge in Amapa State linked to seasonal flooding, precarious sanitation, and transmission in wetland and stilt-house communities 18 , 19 . Despite its prevalence, underreporting persists due to symptomatic overlap with malaria and dengue 20 . Our finding that Leptospira spp. was the second most prevalent confirmed pathogen underscores its critical standing in the regional etiology of AFI. Unlike arboviral infections, which only require supportive care, leptospirosis demands timely antibiotic therapy to prevent severe, potentially fatal complications such as Weil’s disease or pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome. Relying entirely on early clinical differentiation or waiting days for laboratory confirmation in highly endemic zones often results in catastrophic therapeutic delays. Therefore, in areas with high dengue and leptospirosis co-endemicity, clinical protocols must explicitly support the initiation of empirical antibiotic treatment (such as doxycycline or amoxicillin) for patients presenting with severe febrile syndromes and clear epidemiological risk factors, prioritizing clinical survival over definitive laboratory timelines.Parvovirus B19 occurred in 16 cases (7.6%), representing a notable proportion of AFI diagnoses. Its clinical recognition remains challenging as its early symptoms closely mimic arboviruses such as dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. In tropical regions, B19V is often misdiagnosed as dengue due to overlapping presentations of fever, headache, and rash 21 , 22 . The post-pandemic resurgence of B19V in 2024-2025 marked a significant epidemiological shift driven by an “immunity gap” in pediatric populations. IgM positivity peaked at ~40% in children aged 5-9 years and ~10% in adults, complicating AFI differential diagnosis 23 .Of the 727 investigated individuals, viral hepatitis was suspected in 10 cases (1.4%), with three confirmed cases of hepatitis A and B (1.4%). No HEV cases were identified despite evidence that HEV genotype 3 is a zoonotic pathogen of concern in Brazil 24 , 25 .Meta-analyses estimate anti-HEV IgG seroprevalence at ~6% nationally, with regional variations: ~3% in the Amazon and up to 14.2% in rural Rondônia 26 - 28 . Diagnostic invisibility remains a major challenge as public health screening routinely ignores HEV testing, particularly in vulnerable Amazonian populations. Overlapping clinical presentations with hepatitis b and d further obscure HEV detection, suggesting that some acute hepatitis cases of “unknown etiology” may represent undiagnosed HEV.Measles occurred in 15 cases (7.1%). Despite mass vaccination programs, Brazil lost its measles-free status in 2018 following outbreaks linked to Venezuelan migration and low vaccination coverage 29 , 30 . Although elimination status was regained in 2023-2024, new cases in Tocantins in 2025 highlight ongoing vulnerability. The porous border of Amapa State with French Guiana and high mobility of illegal gold miners create a unique epidemiological corridor sustaining measles and other infectious diseases.Malaria transmission remains a major concern in Oiapoque, one of the highest transmission zones in the Americas. Despite persistent “silent” transmission by asymptomatic carriers in mobile populations, our cohort only included two malaria cases (0.95%), reflecting the predominance of samples collected in Macapa. Epidemiological data shows a downward trend in Amapa State, with a 16.8% reduction in cases from 2024 to 2025 and an 82% decline in Macapa. Nonetheless, the Oiapoque border remains the main epidemiological challenge in the state 31 - 34 . The cohort included a case of acute Chagas disease, reflecting the specific epidemiological profile of Amapa State. From 2018 to 2022, the state remained a high-endemicity region for acute Chagas disease in the Brazilian Amazon, with oral transmission—primarily by consumption of artisanal acai and bacaba juice—emerging as the dominant route of infection 35 , 36 .A notable finding in this study was the elevated detection of multiple infectious agents. Across 727 patients, this study found 209 reactive results, with co-detection of distinct pathogens in 23 cases. Similar patterns have been reported in regions endemic for malaria and arboviruses, in which simultaneous infections are confirmed by multiple molecular assays 37 , 38 . In such contexts, potential cross-reactivity further compounds diagnostic complexity. The cross-reactivity between zika, dengue, and yellow fever serological assays, for example, is primarily attributed to the high degree of structural homology within the envelope protein in members of the Orthoflavivirus genus 39 .The seasonal transmission pattern in this study likely reflects the equatorial climate of the region, in which persistently high precipitation and elevated temperatures sustain vector breeding sites throughout the year. full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSThe causes of AFI in Amapa are multiple and may involve infection by more than one etiological agent. This underscores the complexity of diagnostic accuracy in regions with overlapping multiple arbovirus and bacterial transmission. The detection of rare pathogens such as Mayaro virus and acute Chagas disease reflects the unique ecological and epidemiological profile of the region. These findings reinforce the role of Amapa State as a sentinel for infectious disease surveillance as its porous borders, ecological connectivity, and high human mobility sustain transmission corridors. Strengthening laboratory capacity, integrating differential diagnostics, and expanding surveillance systems are essential to capture the true burden of AFI and to guide targeted interventions. While acknowledging the limitations inherent to retrospective designs and diagnostic constraints, this study emphasizes the global relevance of integrated surveillance in ecologically dynamic regions. Crucially, addressing these challenges requires improving data completeness, such as by the meticulous entry and digital optimization of GAL forms, to ensure accurate epidemiological tracking in complex equatorial settings.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONManaging the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of community-acquired acute febrile illness (AFI) constitutes a major public health challenge in Latin America due to its complex epidemiological profile and potentially profound social consequences 1 . A comprehensive understanding of their etiologies is essential for advancing clinical practice, guiding public health strategies, and informing policy development.The ecology of the Amazon basin—characterized by deforestation, flooding, and high vector diversity—creates favorable conditions for arboviruses and bacterial pathogens, amplifying the risk of febrile outbreaks 2 . Thus, the region experiences a wide spectrum of febrile illnesses caused by viral, bacterial, and parasitic agents, reflecting diverse ecological and climatic conditions 3 .The overlapping clinical manifestations of diseases such as dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and rickettsial infections complicate accurate diagnosis. This diagnostic uncertainty often results in delayed or inappropriate treatment. Misdiagnosis may postpone life-saving antibiotic therapy, whereas indiscriminate prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The Pan American Health Organization 4 has emphasized antimicrobial resistance as a regional priority, highlighting its impact on healthcare costs and mortality.Community-acquired AFI contributes substantially to regional morbidity and mortality, considerably straining healthcare systems and requiring significant resource allocation for surveillance and management. Socioeconomic factors, including poverty and limited access to healthcare, exacerbate transmission dynamics and hinder effective disease control 5 .Surveillance represents a critical component of disease control. The Brazilian Amazon is recognized as a global hotspot for emerging viruses 2 . Integrated screening systems may serve as sentinel mechanisms for early detection. As deforestation and mining activities intensify, human populations increasingly encounter novel vectors such as mosquitoes and midges, underscoring the importance of screening febrile patients for malaria and arboviruses6. Without routine screening, outbreaks may remain undetected, manifesting themselves only as “unexplained fevers.”Amapa State, in the Eastern Brazilian Amazon, exemplifies one of the most complex diagnostic environments in the world. While dengue remains a major concern, the unique geography of the state—bordering French Guiana and the Atlantic Ocean, and dominated by dense rainforest and wetlands—heightens the risk of diverse infectious diseases. High rainfall and humidity render leptospirosis endemic, particularly in peri-urban areas such as Macapa and Santana 5 . Recent land-use transformations, including illegal mining and the expansion of acai production, have had measurable epidemiological consequences. These activities are consistently associated with increased malaria incidence due to favorable conditions for Anopheles vectors 6 . Moreover, the commercialization of acai has contributed to the emergence of foodborne transmission of Chagas disease 7 .EthicsThis study was approved by the institutional Research Ethics Committee (CAAE No 53153916.7.0000.0065). All data were anonymized prior to analysis, and access to secondary data from the Laboratory Environment Manager (GAL) and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN) was restricted to variables necessary for epidemiological characterization (with authorization from health surveillance authorities). EthicsThis study was approved by the institutional Research Ethics Committee (CAAE No 53153916.7.0000.0065). All data were anonymized prior to analysis, and access to secondary data from the Laboratory Environment Manager (GAL) and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN) was restricted to variables necessary for epidemiological characterization (with authorization from health surveillance authorities). Laboratory proceduresSpecimens were initially processed at the Central Public Health Laboratory of Amapa State (LACEN-AP) following routine diagnostic protocols, including arbovirus screening when clinically indicated. Additional tests, such as serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for other pathogens, were performed at the discretion of attending physicians, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory local methods included enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (the latter exclusively for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing; for bacterial and fungal infections, ELISA for leptospirosis and blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed; whereas parasitic infections were confirmed using thick blood smears, the Strout test, electrochemiluminescence, and immunochromatographic tests.After initial processing, samples were stored at −20 °C and shipped to the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP, LIM-52), in which they were preserved at −80 °C until further testing. Molecular screeningAt LV-IMT-FMUSP, samples underwent real-time PCR assays targeting viral agents. The screening included assays for Pan-Orthoflavivirus and Pan-Alphavirus. The following viral agents were tested: Flaviviruses, Alphaviruses, Orthobunyaviruses: yellow fever 8 , dengue, zika, chikungunya, mayaro, and oropouche viruses 9 .Genus Orthoflavivirus 10 : Japanese encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Usutu, West Nile, and Saint Louis encephalitis viruses.Genus Alphavirus 11 : Ross River, O’nyong-nyong, Sindbis, Barmah Forest, Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses. Additional real-time PCR assays included pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations, such as enterovirus 12 , parvovirus B19 13 , hepatitis E virus (HEV) 14 , and Leptospira spp 15 . GALIn this study, diagnostic test results from LACEN-AP were retrieved via GAL.GAL, the national computerized system, was designed to manage and monitor laboratory routines within the National Public Health Laboratory Network. It is managed by the Ministry of Health via the General Coordination of Public Health Laboratories and tracks the flow of biological samples from collection to final diagnosis, standardizing results and providing real-time data for the surveillance of high-priority and compulsory notification diseases. SINANSINAN, the primary national surveillance database managed by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, is a decentralized system fed by the mandatory notification of diseases and conditions in the National Compulsory Notification List.SINAN provides high-resolution microdata (individual-level records) that include clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, pregnancy status, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations), diagnostic test results, among others. Integration of dataClinical and demographic variables (age, sex, municipality of residence, reported condition, date of symptom onset, and clinical manifestations) were combined with GAL laboratory results. Using this integrated dataset, data analysis was strictly descriptive, focusing on characterizing the reported cases.For the diagnostic tests either at LACEN or IMT, samples were classified as positive if they were reactive in at least one assay. title_original: Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to identify the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in acute febrile illness (AFI) cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, to better understand the epidemiological landscape of these infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a sentinel surveillance conducted in public health laboratories in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, from 2018 to 2022. It analyzed samples from 727 individuals, with definitive diagnoses obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), including 23 cases of co-infection.
analysis.methods: Diagnostic tests included serology, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and sequencing. Confirmatory methods involved enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and NS1 (for dengue), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing. Data were integrated from clinical and demographic variables with laboratory results from the GAL system.
analysis.main_results: Chikungunya virus was the second most frequent diagnosis after dengue, with 16 cases (7.6%) identified. Other notable findings included leptospirosis (20 cases, 9.5%), measles (15 cases, 7.1%), and parvovirus B19 (16 cases, 7.6%). There were 23 cases of co-infection, with chikungunya virus being involved in 7 cases (43.8%) alongside dengue virus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the significant role of chikungunya virus in the etiology of acute febrile illness in the region, providing insights into its prevalence and co-infection patterns with other pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings contribute to the understanding of the epidemiology of chikungunya virus in the Brazilian Amazon, aiding in the development of targeted surveillance and diagnostic strategies for this region.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its descriptive nature and reliance on routine diagnostic procedures, which may introduce variability in testing methods. The evidence is moderate due to the observational design and potential for confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness (AFI) in the Brazilian Amazon region from 2018 to 2022 to identify potential etiologies. Chikungunya virus was the second most frequent diagnosis, with 16 cases (7.6%) identified, following dengue virus (52%). The study found 23 co-infection cases, with chikungunya virus involved in 7 cases alongside dengue. Methods included serology, PCR, and sequencing, with results integrated from clinical and demographic data. The findings highlight the epidemiological significance of chikungunya virus in the region, supporting targeted surveillance and diagnostic efforts. However, the study's descriptive nature and reliance on routine procedures limit the strength of the evidence, which is assessed as moderate.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在确定巴西阿马帕州亚马逊地区 2018 年至 2022 年报告的急性发热性疾病 (AFI) 病例中病毒和其他感染的潜在病因,以更好地了解这些感染的流行病学状况。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项前哨监测研究于2018年至2022年在巴西阿马帕州亚马逊地区的公共卫生实验室进行。该研究分析了727人的样本,其中185人(25.4%)获得了明确诊断,其中包括23例合并感染病例。
elements_zh.methods: 诊断测试包括 血清学、聚合酶链反应 (PCR) 和测序。验证方法包括免疫球蛋白 M (IgM) 和 NS1(登革热)的酶联免疫吸附测定 (ELISA)、电化学发光、逆转录 PCR (RT-PCR) 和测序。将临床和人口变量数据与 GAL 系统的实验室结果进行整合。
elements_zh.main_results: 基孔肯雅病毒 是继登革热之后第二常见的 诊断,已发现 16 例(7.6%)。其他值得注意的发现包括钩端螺旋体病(20 例,9.5%)、麻疹(15 例,7.1%)和细小病毒 B19(16 例,7.6%)。共有23例合并感染,其中基孔肯雅病毒与登革热病毒一起感染7例(43.8%)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究强调了 基孔肯雅病毒 在该地区急性发热性疾病病因学中的重要作用,提供了对其 患病率 以及与其他病原体的共感染模式的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现有助于了解巴西亚马逊地区的 流行病学 或 基孔肯雅病毒,有助于制定针对该地区的针对性 监测 和诊断策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其描述性性质和对常规诊断程序的依赖而受到限制,这可能会引入测试方法的变异性。由于观察设计和潜在的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在确定巴西阿马帕州亚马逊地区 2018 年至 2022 年报告的急性发热性疾病 (AFI) 病例中病毒和其他感染的潜在病因,以更好地了解这些感染的流行病学状况。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项前哨监测研究于2018年至2022年在巴西阿马帕州亚马逊地区的公共卫生实验室进行。该研究分析了727人的样本,其中185人(25.4%)获得了明确诊断,其中包括23例合并感染病例。
analysis_zh.methods: 诊断测试包括 血清学、聚合酶链反应 (PCR) 和测序。验证方法包括免疫球蛋白 M (IgM) 和 NS1(登革热)的酶联免疫吸附测定 (ELISA)、电化学发光、逆转录 PCR (RT-PCR) 和测序。将临床和人口变量数据与 GAL 系统的实验室结果进行整合。
analysis_zh.main_results: 基孔肯雅病毒 是继登革热之后第二常见的 诊断,已发现 16 例(7.6%)。其他值得注意的发现包括钩端螺旋体病(20 例,9.5%)、麻疹(15 例,7.1%)和细小病毒 B19(16 例,7.6%)。共有23例合并感染,其中基孔肯雅病毒与登革热病毒一起感染7例(43.8%)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究强调了 基孔肯雅病毒 在该地区急性发热性疾病病因学中的重要作用,提供了对其 患病率 以及与其他病原体的共感染模式的见解。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现有助于了解巴西亚马逊地区的 流行病学 或 基孔肯雅病毒,有助于制定针对该地区的针对性 监测 和诊断策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其描述性性质和对常规诊断程序的依赖而受到限制,这可能会引入测试方法的变异性。由于观察设计和潜在的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

title: Updated checklist of Culicidae (Diptera) in Adana Province, Türkiye, with the first record of Aedes albopictus
abstract: Aedes (Ae.) albopictus is an invasive mosquito species of major public health concern due to its ability to transmit arboviruses such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. Although its expansion in Europe and Türkiye is well documented, data from the eastern Mediterranean region remain limited. This study aimed to update the Culicidae fauna of Adana Province and determine the occurrence and establishment status of Ae. albopictus . Field surveys were conducted at 30 sites across urban, peri-urban, agricultural, and coastal habitats in Adana Province, Türkiye, during the summer of 2024. Adult mosquitoes were collected using CDC miniature light traps, while immature stages were sampled from aquatic habitats and reared to adulthood under laboratory conditions. Species identification was performed using standard morphological keys and taxonomic references. A total of 2,130 specimens representing seven mosquito species and four genera were identified. Culex (Cx.) pipiens was the dominant species, whereas Ae. albopictus accounted for 227 individuals (10.64%). The species was detected in all surveyed districts (Seyhan, Yüreğir, Karataş, and Yumurtalık). Both field-collected adults and laboratory-emerged specimens confirmed the presence of all developmental stages, with higher abundance in Seyhan District indicating localized population foci. The detection of multiple life stages provides strong evidence for the establishment of Ae. albopictus in Adana Province, representing a significant southward expansion in Türkiye. These findings fill a critical gap in national distribution data and highlight ongoing invasion dynamics in the eastern Mediterranean region. Enhanced surveillance and integrated vector management are required due to its epidemiological importance.

Page 1/12 Abstract Aedes (Ae.) albopictus is an invasive mosquito species of major public health concern due to its ability to transmit arboviruses such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. Although its expansion in Europe and Türkiye is well documented, data from the eastern Mediterranean region remain limited. This study aimed to update the Culicidae fauna of Adana Province and determine the occurrence and establishment status of Ae. albopictus. Field surveys were conducted at 30 sites across urban, peri-urban, agricultural, and coastal habitats in Adana Province, Türkiye, during the summer of 2024. Adult mosquitoes were collected using CDC miniature light traps, while immature stages were sampled from aquatic habitats and reared to adulthood under laboratory conditions. Species identification was performed using standard morphological keys and taxonomic references. A total of 2,130 specimens representing seven mosquito species and four genera were identified. Culex (Cx.) pipiens was the dominant species, whereas Ae. albopictus accounted for 227 individuals (10.64%). The species was detected in all surveyed districts (Seyhan, Yüreğir, Karataş, and Yumurtalık). Both field-collected adults and laboratory-emerged specimens confirmed the presence of all developmental stages, with higher abundance in Seyhan District indicating localized population foci. The detection of multiple life stages provides strong evidence for the establishment of Ae. albopictus in Adana Province, representing a significant southward expansion in Türkiye. These findings fill a critical gap in national distribution data and highlight ongoing invasion dynamics in the eastern Mediterranean region. Enhanced surveillance and integrated vector management are required due to its epidemiological importance. Introduction Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health challenge, accounting for more than 17% of all infectious diseases and causing over 700,000 deaths annually worldwide. Among arthropod vectors, mosquitoes are considered the most important group from a public health perspective because they transmit a wide range of pathogens responsible for diseases such as malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, West Nile fever, and Zika virus disease (World Health Organization, 2024). Species of the genus Aedes (Ae.) (Diptera: Culicidae) are among the most important mosquito vectors of human arboviruses. In particular, Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are responsible for the transmission of several medically important viruses, including dengue virus (DENV), chikungunya virus (CHIKV), zika virus (ZIKV), and yellow fever virus (YFV). Their close association with human settlements, adaptation to artificial breeding sites, and high ecological plasticity have contributed substantially to their epidemiological importance and global expansion (Bonizzoni et al. 2013; Kraemer et al. 2015). As a consequence of this global expansion, invasive Aedes mosquito populations have shown a marked increase across the European continent in recent decades. To date, at least six non-native mosquito species have been reported as introduced or established in Europe, including Ae. atropalpus, Ae. japonicus, Ae. koreicus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, and Ae. triseriatus (Vasquez et al. 2023). Among invasive mosquito species, Ae. albopictus is considered one of the most rapidly expanding globally, owing to its high ecological plasticity, desiccation-resistant eggs, and ability to survive under temperate climatic conditions (Kraemer et al. 2019). In Europe, this species has been associated with autochthonous outbreaks of dengue in countries including France, Italy, Croatia, and Spain, as well as chikungunya outbreaks in France and Italy, highlighting its established role in local transmission cycles (Kraemer et al. 2019; ECDC, 2026). Consequently, Ae. albopictus is now widely established across large parts of Europe, particularly in Mediterranean and temperate regions, with ongoing geographic expansion. Page 2/12 Furthermore, the public health significance of Aedes mosquitoes is also recognized in neighboring regions such as Türkiye, where Culicidae species have been extensively documented in terms of distribution and vectorial capacity (Şimşek & Günay, 2017). The potential for Zika virus (ZIKV) transmission remains a concern in areas receiving imported cases, as experimental studies have demonstrated that both Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are capable of supporting ZIKV infection and transmission under suitable environmental conditions (Ciota et al. 2017; Gómez et al. 2022). Following its first detection in Türkiye in Edirne in 2011 (Öter et al. 2013), Ae. albopictus has progressively expanded its distribution across the country, with established records reported from the Marmara, Black Sea, and Aegean regions (Demirci et al. 2021; ECDC, 2026). Despite this documented spread, evidence regarding the presence and local establishment of Ae. albopictus in the eastern Mediterranean region of Türkiye, particularly in Adana Province, remained limited prior to recent observations (Şimşek & Yavaşoğlu, 2023). The aim of this study was to investigate the occurrence and field-based distribution of Ae. albopictus in Adana Province, southern Türkiye, and to provide baseline entomological data for future surveillance and risk assessment of this invasive vector species. Methodology Study Area The study was conducted across 30 geographically predefined sites located in the districts of Seyhan, Yüreğir, Sarıçam, Karataş, and Yumurtalık in Adana Province, Türkiye. Sampling sites were distributed across a broad spatial gradient and were georeferenced using GPS coordinates. The study area is situated in the eastern Mediterranean region and is characterized by a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters (Köppen–Geiger classification: Csa). The elevation of the sampling sites ranged from 1 to 88 m above sea level. (Fig. 1). Mosquito Sampling, Rearing and Morphological Identification Mosquito sampling was conducted across diverse ecological settings, including residential areas, agricultural landscapes, and peri-urban environments, all of which are considered suitable habitats for the establishment and persistence of invasive mosquito species such as Ae. albopictus. Field surveys were performed during the summer of 2024 (June–August), and each of the 30 predefined sampling sites was visited three times. At each sampling occasion, collections were conducted over five consecutive days and five nights, ensuring standardized temporal coverage across sites. Adult mosquito sampling was carried out using CDC miniature light traps (Model 512, John W. Hock Company, Gainesville, FL, USA) (Fig. 2A and 2B), which were deployed at each site. Four traps were used per site per sampling event, resulting in a total of 360 trap-night samples across the study area. Traps were positioned at approximately 1.5 m above ground level and operated for 24 h. Specimens collected were preserved in 70% ethanol and transported to the laboratory for further processing. In addition to adult collections, immature stages were surveyed in a variety of natural and artificial aquatic habitats, including irrigation canals, temporary rain pools, stagnant water accumulations, and domestic water storage containers (Fig. 2C-2F). Larvae and pupae were collected using standard larval dippers (Fig. 2G) and transported to the laboratory in labeled containers. Following transport, specimens were maintained in water-filled containers in a sheltered outdoor area within the Faculty of Medicine campus and allowed to complete their development under ambient environmental Page 3/12 conditions. Individuals were monitored regularly until adult emergence, and the emerged adults were subsequently collected for species identification (WHO, 2005; Silver, 2008) (Fig. 2H and 2I). Species identification of both field-collected adults and adults emerging from field-collected immature stages was performed under a stereomicroscope using standard morphological identification keys, including Merdivenci (1984), Şimşek and Günay (2017), and the MosKeyTool interactive identification platform. Results A total of 2,130 mosquito specimens were collected during the study period through direct adult sampling and immature-stage collections followed by laboratory rearing to adulthood. Seven mosquito species belonging to four genera were identified. Species composition analysis showed that Culex (Cx.) pipiens was the predominant species, accounting for 964 specimens (45.23%) of the total collection. The second most abundant species was Cx. territans, represented by 450 specimens (21.13%). Ae. albopictus ranked third in abundance with 227 specimens (10.64%), followed by Ae. caspius with 200 specimens (9.39%). Anopheles maculipennis and Cx. quinquefasciatus accounted for 170 (7.98%) and 110 (5.16%) specimens, respectively, whereas Culiseta morsitans was the least frequently encountered species, represented by only 10 specimens (0.47%). A total of 227 Aedes (Ae.) albopictus specimens were recorded from 30 sampling locations distributed across the Seyhan, Yüreğir, Karataş, and Yumurtalık districts of Adana Province. Of these, 82 specimens were collected as adults in the field using CDC light traps, whereas 145 specimens were obtained through laboratory rearing of immature stages collected from breeding habitats. The species was detected across all four surveyed districts and was recorded from a variety of habitat types, including urban residential areas, peri-urban settlements, agricultural zones, and coastal localities. The highest abundances were observed in Seyhan District, particularly in Çamlıtepe, where 14 field-collected adults and 18 reared adults were obtained, and in Balcalı, where 11 field-collected adults and 14 reared adults were recorded. Additional positive sampling sites were distributed across Yüreğir, Karataş, and Yumurtalık districts. The spatial distribution of Ae. albopictus across sampling locations is presented in Table 1. Adult and laboratory-emerged adult specimens of Ae. albopictus were confirmed based on direct morphological examination under a stereomicroscope. Diagnostic characters observed included a black integument with a distinct longitudinal median stripe of silvery-white scales on the scutum, dark legs with white tarsal banding, and abdominal tergites with pale scale patches consistent with species-level diagnostic morphology. These characters were consistently observed in both field-collected adults and laboratory-emerged specimens, supporting species-level identification of Ae. albopictus from multiple sampling sites. The morphological characteristics of adult specimens are illustrated in Fig. 3. Discussion The present study provides the first confirmed record of Aedes (Ae.) albopictus in Adana Province, representing a significant southward extension of the known distribution of this invasive mosquito species in Türkiye. Since its initial detection in northwestern Türkiye in 2011 (Oter et al. 2013), Ae. albopictus has exhibited a progressive range expansion across the country, with established populations reported from the Black Sea and Aegean regions (Akiner et al. 2016; Şimşek and Günay, 2017; Demirci et al. 2021). However, prior to the present study, records from the eastern Mediterranean region remained absent, indicating a notable geographical gap in its documented distribution. The detection of Ae. albopictus in Adana therefore fills an important spatial discontinuity and confirms further expansion toward southern Türkiye. Page 4/12 The establishment of Ae. albopictus in Adana is consistent with its well-documented ecological plasticity and adaptation to anthropogenic environments. The species is known to exploit artificial water containers, irrigation systems, and urban drainage structures, which facilitate population persistence in Mediterranean-type cities (Benedict et al. 2007; Bonizzoni et al. 2013; Ravasi et al. 2022). Additionally, the production of desiccation-resistant eggs enhances survival under seasonal climatic variability, promoting long-term establishment in temperate and semi-arid environments. Climatic suitability assessments further indicate that southern Türkiye provides favorable conditions for colonization due to extended warm seasons and increasing temperatures (Caminade et al. 2012; Merkenschlager et al. 2025). The simultaneous detection of field-collected adults and individuals emerging from laboratory-reared immature stages provides strong evidence of local reproduction and establishment of Ae. albopictus populations. In vector ecology, the presence of immature stages in breeding habitats is widely recognized as an indicator of autochthonous populations and sustained local reproduction (Pedric et al. 2014). The successful emergence of adults from field-collected immature stages further confirms that developmental completion occurs under local environmental conditions, indicating active and viable breeding populations. European surveillance frameworks similarly apply the presence of multiple life stages as a criterion to distinguish transient introductions from established populations (Medlock et al. 2012). Collectively, these observations support the presence of a self-sustaining Ae. albopictus population in the study area. Although the exact introduction pathway remains uncertain, human-mediated transport is the most plausible mechanism. The global spread of Ae. albopictus has been strongly associated with the trade of used tires and ornamental plants, as well as maritime transport networks (Benedict et al. 2007; Bonizzoni et al. 2013; Willoughby et al. 2024). In the context of southern Türkiye, major port activities and regional transport corridors may have facilitated repeated introductions and secondary dispersal. While these hypotheses require molecular validation, they are consistent with the known invasion biology of the species. The establishment of Ae. albopictus in Adana has important public health implications. Although no autochthonous dengue or chikungunya transmission has been reported in Türkiye, the presence of competent vectors constitutes a prerequisite for local transmission. Increasing reports of autochthonous arboviral outbreaks in southern Europe highlight the growing epidemiological relevance of Ae. albopictus in temperate regions (Viginier et al. 2024). Introduction Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health challenge, accounting for more than 17% of all infectious diseases and causing over 700,000 deaths annually worldwide. Among arthropod vectors, mosquitoes are considered the most important group from a public health perspective because they transmit a wide range of pathogens responsible for diseases such as malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, West Nile fever, and Zika virus disease (World Health Organization, 2024). Species of the genus Aedes (Ae.) (Diptera: Culicidae) are among the most important mosquito vectors of human arboviruses. In particular, Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are responsible for the transmission of several medically important viruses, including dengue virus (DENV), chikungunya virus (CHIKV), zika virus (ZIKV), and yellow fever virus (YFV). Their close association with human settlements, adaptation to artificial breeding sites, and high ecological plasticity have contributed substantially to their epidemiological importance and global expansion (Bonizzoni et al. 2013; Kraemer et al. 2015). As a consequence of this global expansion, invasive Aedes mosquito populations have shown a marked increase across the European continent in recent decades. To date, at least six non-native mosquito species have been reported as introduced or established in Europe, including Ae. atropalpus, Ae. japonicus, Ae. koreicus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, and Ae. triseriatus (Vasquez et al. 2023). Among invasive mosquito species, Ae. albopictus is considered one of the most rapidly expanding globally, owing to its high ecological plasticity, desiccation-resistant eggs, and ability to survive under temperate climatic conditions (Kraemer et al. 2019). In Europe, this species has been associated with autochthonous outbreaks of dengue in countries including France, Italy, Croatia, and Spain, as well as chikungunya outbreaks in France and Italy, highlighting its established role in local transmission cycles (Kraemer et al. 2019; ECDC, 2026). Consequently, Ae. albopictus is now widely established across large parts of Europe, particularly in Mediterranean and temperate regions, with ongoing geographic expansion. Page 2/12 Furthermore, the public health significance of Aedes mosquitoes is also recognized in neighboring regions such as Türkiye, where Culicidae species have been extensively documented in terms of distribution and vectorial capacity (Şimşek & Günay, 2017). The potential for Zika virus (ZIKV) transmission remains a concern in areas receiving imported cases, as experimental studies have demonstrated that both Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are capable of supporting ZIKV infection and transmission under suitable environmental conditions (Ciota et al. 2017; Gómez et al. 2022). Following its first detection in Türkiye in Edirne in 2011 (Öter et al. 2013), Ae. albopictus has progressively expanded its distribution across the country, with established records reported from the Marmara, Black Sea, and Aegean regions (Demirci et al. 2021; ECDC, 2026). Despite this documented spread, evidence regarding the presence and local establishment of Ae. albopictus in the eastern Mediterranean region of Türkiye, particularly in Adana Province, remained limited prior to recent observations (Şimşek & Yavaşoğlu, 2023). The aim of this study was to investigate the occurrence and field-based distribution of Ae. albopictus in Adana Province, southern Türkiye, and to provide baseline entomological data for future surveillance and risk assessment of this invasive vector species. Sampling sites were distributed across a broad spatial gradient and were georeferenced using GPS coordinates. The study area is situated in the eastern Mediterranean region and is characterized by a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters (Köppen–Geiger classification: Csa). The elevation of the sampling sites ranged from 1 to 88 m above sea level. (Fig. 1). Mosquito Sampling, Rearing and Morphological Identification Mosquito sampling was conducted across diverse ecological settings, including residential areas, agricultural landscapes, and peri-urban environments, all of which are considered suitable habitats for the establishment and persistence of invasive mosquito species such as Ae. albopictus. Field surveys were performed during the summer of 2024 (June–August), and each of the 30 predefined sampling sites was visited three times. At each sampling occasion, collections were conducted over five consecutive days and five nights, ensuring standardized temporal coverage across sites. Adult mosquito sampling was carried out using CDC miniature light traps (Model 512, John W. Hock Company, Gainesville, FL, USA) (Fig. 2A and 2B), which were deployed at each site. Four traps were used per site per sampling event, resulting in a total of 360 trap-night samples across the study area. Traps were positioned at approximately 1.5 m above ground level and operated for 24 h. Specimens collected were preserved in 70% ethanol and transported to the laboratory for further processing. In addition to adult collections, immature stages were surveyed in a variety of natural and artificial aquatic habitats, including irrigation canals, temporary rain pools, stagnant water accumulations, and domestic water storage containers (Fig. 2C-2F).
